headline: Heavy rain for second day cripples Dhaka with waterlogging
summary: Persistent downpours have submerged major roads, causing severe traffic congestion and widespread suffering for commuters across the capital.
details: Persistent rain since morning has waterlogged large parts of Dhaka, disrupting traffic and causing widespread suffering for office-goers and students.
Several major roads and residential streets went under water, slowing traffic and making movement difficult across the capital.
Commuters are enduring long traffic jams, soaring transport fares, and long waits for buses, rickshaws, and CNG-run auto-rickshaws.
Waterlogging was reported in Green Road, Tejturi Bazar, Panthapath, Bashundhara Residential Area, Monipur, Dhanmondi, Mohammadpur, Shewrapara, Kalshi, and Uttara.
The situation was worsened by rainwater remaining from yesterday's downpour, with knee-deep water in several low-lying areas.
Pedestrians waded through flooded streets, while vehicles crawled through submerged roads, splashing those on foot.
The Gulshan Traffic Division of the DMP reported disruptions on the road adjacent to Dhaka Gate and at the exit ramp of the Banani-Kakoli Elevated Expressway.
Traffic also slowed in the ECB Chattar area and in front of Jamuna Future Park due to accumulated rainwater and WASA pipeline work.
The Gulshan Traffic Division warned that continued rainfall could worsen the situation and advised residents to allow extra travel time.
caption:
Dhaka is underwater again. Persistent rain for a second day has left the capital's roads submerged and commuters stranded.

headline_marked: First time in history: [[Injured tigress released back into Sundarbans]]
headline: First time in history: Injured tigress released back into Sundarbans
summary: After six months of intensive medical care, a tigress trapped in a poacher's snarey was successfully returned to the wild.
details: A tigress, aged 10-11 years, was released back into the Sundarbans on Sunday. This marks the first successful rescue and release of a wild animal in the history of Bangladesh's wildlife conservation.

The tigress had been trapped in a poacher's snare in the early January of this year in the the Chandpai range of the Sundarbans East Forest Division. She was rescued by forest officials using a tranquilizer gun and moved to a rehabilitation center in Khulna.

At the time of rescue, the tigress was skeletal and had severe injuries to her front left leg, where skin, muscle, and veins were damaged. The wounds had become necrotic due to the repeated pulling of the snare rope.
Recovery was a challenging process. Forest officials noted that the initial antibiotics were not enough, as the tigress would scratch at the wounds once they began to heal, causing further bleeding.
A breakthrough occurred in March when, following expert advice, honey was applied to the bandages. This helped the muscle tissue regenerate and the others wounds to dry up.

To ensure she was fit for the wild, the tigress was fed a diet of liver and later live prey, such as pigs, to regain her hunting agility. She was only released after she demonstrated the ability to kill prey within seconds.
The tigress was transported from Khulna to the Mongla fuel jetty and then by launch to the Shala river near the Andharmanik Eco-tourism center, where she was released.

Following the release, a team led by Professor M.A. Aziz of Jahangirnagar University monitored her footprints. They observed that she quickly adapted to her old territory, moving approximately 150 meters into the forest.

The tigress had been trapped in a poacher's snare in the early January of this year in the the Chandpai range of the Sundarbans East Forest Division. She was rescued by forest officials using a tranquilizer gun and moved to a rehabilitation center in Khulna.

At the time of rescue, the tigress was skeletal and had severe injuries to her front left leg, where skin, muscle, and veins were damaged. The wounds had become necrotic due to the repeated pulling of the snare rope.

Recovery was a challenging process. Forest officials noted that the initial antibiotics were not enough, as the tigress would scratch at the wounds once they began to heal, causing further bleeding.

A breakthrough occurred in March when, following expert advice, honey was applied to the bandages. This helped the muscle tissue regenerate and the others wounds to dry up.

To ensure she was fit for the wild, the tigress was fed a diet of liver and later live prey, such as pigs, to regain her hunting agility. She was only released after she demonstrated the ability to kill prey within seconds.

The tigress was transported from Khulna to the Mongla fuel jetty and then by launch to the Shala river near the Andharmanik Eco-tourism center, where she was released.
